title: Mathematical Reasoning
tagline: Year 2 — New operations, missing signs, interchanged symbols and inequality chains

introduction.overview: Mathematical reasoning questions test whether you can follow rules that are stated in the question. Typical forms: a new operation is defined (a ◈ b = a² + b) and you evaluate expressions with it; signs are missing in an equation and you find them; two signs or numbers are interchanged and you evaluate; or a chain of inequalities is given and you decide which relation follows. The arithmetic is simple; accuracy in applying the rule is what matters.
introduction.placementRelevance: Mathematical reasoning questions are commonly asked in company reasoning rounds. They are quick if you follow the rule literally and check with BODMAS.
introduction.realWorldContext: Spreadsheet formulas, code functions and unit conversions are defined operations in just this way.

learningObjectives: Evaluate expressions with a newly defined operation
Find missing arithmetic signs by systematic trial
Evaluate after interchanging signs or numbers
Draw conclusions from chains of inequalities

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: BODMAS: Brackets, Orders, Division and Multiplication (left to right), Addition and Subtraction (left to right). In a chain a > b ≥ c = d, a > d holds because one strict step is enough.

coreDefinitions: Defined operation: a rule such as a ◈ b = a² + b that tells you how to combine two numbers.
Interchange of signs/numbers: swap them in the expression before evaluating.
Missing signs: choose operators from +, −, ×, ÷ so that the equation is true.
Inequality chain: a series of relations (>, ≥, <, ≤, =) linking quantities.
Conclusion from a chain: valid if it holds in every case consistent with the chain.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: The rule is a machine: put numbers in, follow the instructions, take the result out. Never mix the new rule with ordinary arithmetic. In a defined operation, the letters a and b stand for the left and right entries in order.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Write the rule, replace a and b with the actual numbers in the right order, evaluate inside brackets first, and then apply the rule again if the expression is nested.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Defined operation
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Replace a and b by the given numbers, in order
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Order matters: a ◈ b is not b ◈ a in general.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Nested operations
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: (5 Δ 3) Δ 2 with a² − b²: 16 Δ 2 = 252

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Missing signs
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Try the 16 pairs of signs and test with BODMAS

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Interchange
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Swap the named symbols or numbers, then evaluate

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Inequality chain
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: a > b ≥ c = d ⇒ a > d
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: A chain with at least one strict sign gives strict.

mainNarrative: For a defined operation, copy the rule and substitute. If a ◈ b = a² + b, then 3 ◈ 4 = 3² + 4 = 13. The order matters: 4 ◈ 3 = 16 + 3 = 19. For nested expressions, work from the inside out.
For missing signs, try combinations systematically. For 8 _ 2 _ 4 = 12, test: 8 × 2 − 4 = 16 − 4 = 12, which works. Always apply BODMAS: multiplication before subtraction.
For interchange, swap first. If + and × are interchanged, then 6 + 3 × 2 becomes 6 × 3 + 2 = 20. If the numbers 4 and 7 are interchanged in 4 × 3 + 7, the expression becomes 7 × 3 + 4 = 25.
For inequality chains, combine links. P > Q ≥ R = S gives P > S, because P > Q ≥ R and R = S. A chain gives a conclusion between its ends only when the signs point the same way.
For equation-based definitions, solve for the unknown. If a ★ b = 3a − 2b and x ★ 4 = 10, then 3x − 8 = 10, so x = 6.

deepDiveAspects.title: Non-commutative operations
deepDiveAspects.content: Most defined operations are not commutative: a ◈ b differs from b ◈ a. Respect the order given.

deepDiveAspects.title: Checking by substitution
deepDiveAspects.content: After finding a missing sign or an unknown, substitute back to verify the equation.

solvedExamples.title: Defined operation
solvedExamples.question: If a ◈ b = a² + b, find 3 ◈ 4.

solvedExamples.title: Missing signs
solvedExamples.question: Which pair of signs fills 8 _ 2 _ 4 = 12?

steps.title: Check others
steps.explanation: For example + , × gives 8 + 8 = 16; not equal to 12.

solvedExamples.commonTrap: Evaluating left to right ignoring BODMAS.

solvedExamples.title: Inequality chain
solvedExamples.question: If P > Q ≥ R = S, which relation between P and S is certain?

steps.title: Combine
steps.explanation: P > Q ≥ S, so P > S.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: One strict sign makes the chain strict.

shortcutMethods.title: Literal substitution

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Reason about the rule in words.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Rewrite the rule with the actual numbers in order, evaluate with BODMAS, and verify by substitution.

rulesForApplication: Respect the order of a and b.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Test options by substituting into the stated rule.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Write the rule at the top of the page.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: These are among the fastest reasoning items.

selfCheckQuestions: Can I evaluate a defined operation?
Can I read an inequality chain?
